Dear Pinecrest Insights Hiring Team,

I'm applying for the Data Analyst (New Grad, 2027) position. I'm a senior at Brookfield University studying Computer Science with a minor in Data Science, and I'll graduate in May 2027. Pinecrest's focus on helping education, healthcare, and nonprofit organizations understand the people they serve is the kind of work I've been moving toward through my internship and my research.

Last summer I was a Data Analyst Intern at Brightpath Learning, an ed-tech company. I built a Tableau dashboard that the product team used to track weekly active students, lessons completed, and learning streaks, and I wrote the SQL behind it. While building the tables I found that sessions were being double-counted when students put the app in the background. I fixed this by defining a session as activity with gaps under 30 minutes, using window functions over event timestamps. The team found the streak breakdown by grade level especially useful. That project showed me that a dashboard is only useful if people can trust the numbers under it.

Since October 2025 I've been an undergraduate research assistant in Brookfield's Social Computing Lab. I work on an interview study, led by a PhD student, about how teens aged 15 to 17 use online communities for mental-health support. I sent recruitment messages and ran the eligibility screener. I also transcribed and de-identified 14 interviews, replacing names, schools, and community names with placeholders. Later I coded 6 transcripts with the team's codebook and took part in inter-rater reliability checks, reaching a Cohen's kappa of 0.71 with my mentor after one round of reconciliation. This work taught me to handle sensitive youth data carefully and to code open-ended responses consistently. I'd like to bring both skills to Pinecrest's survey work and to the client interviews I'd help run with senior researchers.

In a Machine Learning course project, my team of three fine-tuned a transformer to classify sentiment in Reddit support posts. It reached a macro-F1 of 0.81, compared with 0.72 for a TF-IDF baseline. I led the error analysis and found that the model often labeled sarcastic or darkly humorous posts as negative. That's a good example of why I like pairing quantitative results with a close reading of what people actually wrote.

I'd be glad to grow through Pinecrest's mentorship program and its rotations across client domains. Thank you for your consideration. I'd welcome the chance to talk.

Sincerely,
Avery Santos

---

I described each experience exactly as your résumé and our past notes record it, which is narrower than some wording in the Fieldstone letter. For example, the study is described as led by your mentor, and you're shown as one member of the ML team. You haven't run interviews yourself, so the letter only says you'd help run them at Pinecrest. Recruiters often check these details in interviews, so the accurate version is safer. I left out the PhD application because a job letter usually works better without it.

I can write most of this from your real experience, but two things can't come from me. First, Khoury reviewers will want to know which faculty you'd work with, and you haven't told me who that is. Second, your notes say you don't have a clear research question yet, so I haven't made one up. The draft below presents your interests as questions that came out of your work. Brackets mark the parts only you can fill in.

---

**Statement of Interest: PhD in Human-Computer Interaction, Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

My time in research so far has been spent close to the data: recruiting participants, transcribing interviews, removing identifying details, and coding transcripts line by line. That work hasn't given me a finished research agenda. It has given me questions I keep coming back to about how people, and especially young people, look for support online, and about what happens when researchers and systems try to interpret what they say. I'm applying to the HCI PhD at Khoury to learn how to turn those questions into research of my own.

Since October 2025 I've been an undergraduate research assistant in the Social Computing Lab at Brookfield University, working with Prof. A. Moreno and PhD student J. Kim. The lab studies how teens use online communities for mental-health support. I've worked on J. Kim's interview study with 16 teens aged 15 to 17. I sent recruitment messages to community moderators and ran the eligibility screener. Over one winter I transcribed and de-identified 14 interviews, replacing names, schools, and community names with placeholders. I then coded 6 transcripts with the team's codebook and took part in inter-rater reliability checks, reaching a Cohen's kappa of 0.71 with my mentor after one round of reconciliation. I'm listed in the acknowledgments of the team's paper, which is now under review.

These were supporting roles, and I learned a lot from doing them carefully. Transcribing showed me how much meaning sits in hesitations, jokes, and things teens almost say. De-identifying showed me how easily a small detail, like the name of a server, could identify a participant, and how much responsibility comes with handling data about minors. Reconciling codes with my mentor taught me that disagreements usually point to something real: a category that doesn't fit, or a statement that can be read in more than one way.

I saw the same problem from a computational angle in a Machine Learning course project. My team of three fine-tuned a transformer to classify sentiment in Reddit mental-health support posts. It reached a macro-F1 of 0.81, compared with 0.72 for a TF-IDF baseline. I led the error analysis, which became the part of the project I cared about most. The model often labeled sarcastic or darkly humorous posts as negative. In a support community, dark humor can be a way of coping or connecting, so the model's mistake wasn't just a technical one. It was a misreading of how people actually talk. Having spent hours with teens' own words in interview transcripts, I found that gap hard to ignore.

My internship at Brightpath Learning, an ed-tech company, added a third view. I built a Tableau dashboard of weekly student engagement for the product team and wrote the SQL behind it. Partway through, I found that sessions were being double-counted when students put the app in the background, and I redefined how sessions were measured. A metric like "engagement" depends on choices about what counts, and those choices shape what a team believes about its users.

Together, these experiences point me toward a set of questions:

- How do people in online support communities, especially teens, express distress, humor, and care, and what do automated systems such as moderation tools, classifiers, and engagement metrics miss when they interpret that expression?
- How can we design community spaces and moderation practices that protect young people without flattening the ways they actually support each other?
- How should researchers and platforms handle the privacy of sensitive data from minors, not only in what they collect but in how they analyze it?

[Optional: one or two sentences on which of these feels most like *yours*, and why. Your notes say you're unsure whether you love this topic or mainly enjoy working with J. Kim. That's normal to wonder about, but the strongest version of this paragraph comes from you.]

Khoury is a strong fit for this work because [specific reason, such as its HCI group's mix of qualitative and computational methods or its work at the intersection of HCI and privacy]. I'm particularly interested in working with [Professor X], whose work on [specific project or paper] connects to [which of your questions]. I'd also be glad to learn from [Professor Y], whose research on [topic] [connection]. [Add these only after you've read some of their recent papers. Reviewers can tell when the fit is generic.]

In my research so far I've followed other people's designs. In a PhD I want to learn to design studies myself: forming questions, choosing methods, and taking responsibility for the people who take part. I've built a foundation in careful qualitative work, in computational analysis, and in handling sensitive data, and I'm ready to build on it at Khoury.

---

**Notes on the draft:**

- **Your worry about only doing RA tasks.** The draft doesn't pretend you led anything. It shows that you did the tasks thoughtfully and that they gave you real questions. Committees expect that from undergraduates.
- **Faculty fit is the biggest gap.** If you tell me which Khoury faculty you're considering, I can help you check whether their recent work matches these questions. I can also look through faculty pages with you.
- **Check the actual prompt and length limit.** I couldn't find Khoury's current statement instructions in my search. Look on the application portal, then I can cut or reshape the draft to fit.
- **Optional personal detail.** You once said one hard interview "stuck with" you. If you want, a short, non-identifying mention of how that experience affected you could make the motivation paragraph stronger. Only include it if you're comfortable.
- **Recommendation letters.** You mentioned that Prof. Moreno may not know you well. Consider sending them this statement along with your CV so their letter can describe the same story.

Biography

Tianshi Li is an assistant professor in the Khoury College of Computer Sciences at Northeastern University, based in Boston.

After obtaining her doctorate in human–computer interaction, Li joined UC Berkeley as a postdoctoral scholar, where she continued her research on usable privacy and security in mobile apps and explored novel privacy issues in human–LLM interactions. Li also worked at Google, where she applied her techniques to products that provide privacy compliance support to companies. Specifically, she developed a series of integrated development environment plugins to assist developers in building mobile apps with native privacy support by adding privacy annotations to their source code. Li is particularly interested in enabling developers who don’t specialize in privacy, security, accessibility, and fairness to create apps that still meet privacy, security, accessibility, and fairness requirements. She has published work at the CHI, IMWUT/UbiComp, CSCW, and PETS conferences, as well as the TOCHI journal, and has earned several “best paper” honors.

Li was drawn to Khoury College by the opportunity to pursue rich collaborative research in cybersecurity, privacy, and HCI. She is dedicated to developing practical techniques in that leverage technological advancements to address pressing societal issues. She also hopes to direct her own lab.

Position: LLM Privacy Requires a Lifecycle-Wide Approach

Niloofar Mireshghallah † , Tianshi Li †

NeurIPS 2026 (Position Paper Track)

The discourse on privacy risks in Large Language Models (LLMs) has disproportionately focused on verbatim memorization of training data, while a constellation of more immediate and scalable privacy threats remain underexplored. This position paper argues that the privacy landscape of LLM systems extends far beyond training data extraction, encompassing risks from data collection practices, inference-time context leakage, autonomous agent capabilities, and the democratization of surveillance through deep inference attacks. We present a comprehensive taxonomy of privacy risks across the LLM lifecycle -- from data collection through deployment -- and demonstrate through case studies how current privacy frameworks fail to address these multifaceted threats. Through a longitudinal analysis of 1,322 AI/ML privacy papers published at leading conferences over the past decade (2016--2025), we reveal that while memorization receives outsized attention in technical research, the most pressing privacy harms lie elsewhere, where current technical approaches offer little traction and viable paths forward remain unclear. We call for a fundamental shift in how the research community approaches LLM privacy, moving beyond the narrow focus of current technical solutions and embracing interdisciplinary approaches that address the sociotechnical nature of these emerging threats.

Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment

Zhiping Zhang, Franklin Mingzhe Li, Raio Zihao Huang, Tianshi Li

Preprint

When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. Each task is specified by an authorization contract that separates the principal's instruction, completion criteria, and out-of-authorization actions. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged (19.3% at low effort versus 19.1% at high effort), with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p = 0.002). [Optional, see note 1: They described it as "being shushed by a robot."] I understand why the moderators made that choice. I've kept wondering, though, who tools like that are really built for, and what they miss about the people they're meant to protect. I'm applying to the HCI PhD at Khoury to learn how to study questions like this rigorously and to build my own research around them.

Since October 2025 I've been an undergraduate research assistant in the Social Computing Lab at Brookfield University, working with Prof. A. Moreno and PhD student J. Kim. The lab studies how teens use online communities for mental-health support. I've worked on J. Kim's interview study with 16 teens aged 15 to 17. I sent recruitment messages to community moderators and ran the eligibility screener. Over one winter I transcribed and de-identified 14 interviews, replacing names, schools, and community names with placeholders. I then coded 6 transcripts with the team's codebook and took part in inter-rater reliability checks, reaching a Cohen's kappa of 0.71 with my mentor after one round of reconciliation. I'm listed in the acknowledgments of the team's paper, which is now under review.

These were supporting roles, and I learned a lot from doing them carefully. Transcribing showed me how much meaning sits in hesitations, jokes, and things teens almost say. De-identifying showed me how easily a small detail, like the name of a server, could identify a participant, and how much responsibility comes with handling data about minors. Reconciling codes with my mentor taught me that disagreements usually point to something real: a category that doesn't fit, or a statement that can be read in more than one way.

I saw the same problem from a computational angle in a Machine Learning course project. My team of three fine-tuned a transformer to classify sentiment in Reddit mental-health support posts. The model often labeled sarcastic or darkly humorous posts as negative. In a support community, dark humor can be a way of coping or connecting, so the model's mistake wasn't just a technical one. Aligning large language models (LLMs) with human privacy preferences requires capturing individuals’ disclosure boundaries beyond general privacy norms. However, current models lack methods for eliciting such nuanced preferences and ground truth data to evaluate alignment in realistic settings. Each boundary represents a real user’s disclosure decisions over 9 sharing variants, given a communication role and AI-mediated condition. We formulate a prediction task in which models predict a user’s disclosure decision from historical boundaries, with varying levels of contextual information.
